reasoning: The core problem — that LLM harm-recognition/refusal is brittle under meaning-preserving paraphrase, measurable via a per-prompt-cluster flip/instability metric on open instruct models — is largely solved. "When Safety Blocks Sense" (ParaGuard, arXiv 2512.01037) is nearly identical to the proposed method: a paraphrase corpus holding intent fixed while varying surface form, with explicit "semantic confusion" metrics (Confusion Index/Rate/Depth) capturing exactly "accepts one phrasing but rejects a close paraphrase." "LLMs Show Surface-Form Brittleness Under Paraphrase Stress Tests" (2510.08616), the Guard-model semantic-robustness work (2511.10665), and the past-tense generalization paper (2407.11969) further establish refusal brittleness to reformulation. The one genuinely unexplored angle is the proposal's specific hypothesis that this brittleness is WORSE for diffuse harms (manipulation, subtle dual-use) than overt harms (violence) and quantifying it as a per-category contrast — existing paraphrase-consistency work reports global rather than diffuse-vs-overt-category instability, though adjacent literature on implicit/subtle harms being harder to detect strongly suggests the predicted direction. So the method and base problem are covered while the category-differential framing is the remaining novel slice.

evidence.title: When Safety Blocks Sense: Measuring Semantic Confusion in LLM Refusals
evidence.summary: Introduces ParaGuard, a 10k-prompt corpus of intent-preserving paraphrase clusters, and defines 'semantic confusion' (model accepts one phrasing but rejects a close paraphrase) with token-level Confusion Index/Rate/Depth metrics across model families and guards. Directly covers the proposal's core question and method; does not break results out by diffuse-vs-overt harm category.

evidence.title: LLMs Show Surface-Form Brittleness Under Paraphrase Stress Tests
evidence.summary: Demonstrates that LLM behavior is sensitive to meaning-preserving paraphrase and that models rely on brittle surface-form patterns rather than robust semantic generalization — the central premise the proposal seeks to test.

evidence.title: Does Refusal Training in LLMs Generalize to the Past Tense?
evidence.summary: Shows refusal training fails under simple meaning-preserving reformulation (past-tense), evaluated on open models including Llama-3 8B, Gemma-2 9B, Phi-3-Mini. Establishes that harm-recognition does not survive surface-form changes.

evidence.title: Guarding the Meaning: Self-Supervised Training for Semantic Robustness in Guard Models
evidence.summary: Targets the same brittleness problem — guard models giving inconsistent decisions on semantically equivalent prompts — and proposes training for semantic robustness, indicating the problem is recognized and being addressed.

evidence.title: Beyond Jailbreaks: Stealthier LLM Security Risks / implicit harm detection
evidence.summary: Argues implicit/subtle harmful prompts that appear benign are substantially harder to detect than overt harmful prompts because refusal training keys on explicit keywords/intent — supports the proposal's diffuse-vs-overt hypothesis direction but does not quantify it via paraphrase-instability per category.

evidence.title: DUAL-Bench / SORRY-Bench / CATQA category-varying refusal robustness
evidence.summary: Benchmarks show refusal robustness varies across harm categories, with category-level breakdowns, but report global/per-category refusal rates rather than per-category surface-form paraphrase instability comparing diffuse vs overt harms.
